claims.text: Bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be produced through a sintering route.
The modeled bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Sintered HfNbTaTiZr contains processing-induced defects typical of bulk specimens.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr occupies interstitial sites and produces associated lattice disorder.
A machine-learning correction should explicitly represent scattering from defects and oxygen interstitials and be calibrated using conductivity measurements.
Electrical-conductivity measurements are available for HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Defect-induced electron localization and scattering dominate conductivity in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering coexists with defect contributions in the 300–1200 K regime.
The distribution of oxygen interstitials and related lattice defects alters electronic conduction pathways through localized-state formation and enhanced scattering.
Including oxygen-related defect scattering changes the modeled effective electron mean free path.
At low temperatures, defects cause stronger electron scattering than perfect-crystal models predict.
At high temperatures, defect–phonon interactions modify electron–phonon coupling.
A machine-learning model trained on experimental data can capture deviations caused by defects that idealized analytical models miss.
The defect-aware model will predict conductivity within approximately ±10% of measurements in both specified temperature regimes.
The defect-aware model will be more accurate than conventional analytical models based on defect-free crystals.
Defect-free analytical models are likely to overestimate low-temperature conductivity.
Defect-free analytical models are likely to misestimate the high-temperature dependence of conductivity.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen contents up to about 1 wt.% and defect densities typical of sintered or additively manufactured specimens.
The model's validity is uncertain for substantially higher oxygen contents or different defect types.
Failure to achieve approximately ±10% accuracy in both regimes, or failure to improve significantly over the conventional model, would falsify the hypothesis.
